title: Chapter 207 – The Silent Terrace
html:
[Terrace Four – Hua]

They cover the Ferryman's empty cloak with a corner of Jian's own, and no one says anything for a very long time.

The boat lies against the quay, rocking gently on a swell that has no source. The lamps along the landing are all dark. The little black glass bell is silent in Mo Yan's fist. Jian sits on the thwart with his staff across his knees and his shaking hands loose in his lap, looking at nothing, and Hua, watching him, thinks that she has never seen a man look so entirely like a person who has been told the price of a thing after buying it.

"He did not say what the fare would be," she says at last, very softly. "For the next crossing."

"A year."

"For each of us."

"For each of us, per leg." He rubs his face with both hands. "There are five legs to the Ninth Terrace after this. Perhaps six. Between the three of us that is eighteen years. If Pebble counts, twenty-four."

"Pebble says she will walk."

"Pebble cannot walk a hundred years." A dry, exhausted breath of a laugh. "And neither can I. I have ninety-two."

She does not answer. There is nothing to say. She looks at the empty cloak, the long black pole lying across the thwarts, the unlit lamps.

"I will pay mine," she says. "And Mo Yan's."

"No."

"Jian—"

"You are a hundred and four." His voice is level. "You told me so yourself, on the quay. Body forty-one, pattern six hundred and thirty-one. You have spent six hundred years in a glass bed. You have no more reason to be generous with your years than I have."

"I have a daughter."

"You do." His eyes meet hers. "And you will keep her. That is what the years are for."

She looks at him a long moment. The shake in his hands has not stopped. The silver line down his jaw has widened to a thread of pale metal. He is the youngest person she knows, and he is the only one who has made her feel old.

"Then who pays?" she says.

"The road." He gets to his feet, slowly, with the staff. "We are going to ask it, politely, to let us walk the next leg. And if it says no, we will think of something else."

"Something stupid."

"Probably." The ghost of a grin crosses his face. "I have been told I am good at those."

The first thing Hua learns on the Fourth Terrace is that her own breath is too loud.

It is a small, shameful discovery. She steps off the dead Ferryman's boat onto a quay of pale gray stone and hears her own boots strike the slabs, and the sound goes out from her like a stone thrown into deep water. It does not echo. It does not fade. It simply goes, and as it goes the stone beneath her feet seems to ripple, ever so faintly, as though she had set down her heel on the back of something that was only pretending to be asleep.

She stops. She holds her breath.

Jian, behind her, has gone absolutely still. His staff is raised a few inches off the quay. His eyes are fixed on a point in the middle distance, and his face has the blank unfocused look it wears when the Interface is speaking. Pebble clings to his shoulder with every claw out. Mo Yan, between them, has pressed both hands over her mouth.

Do not speak, Hua thinks. She does not know why. She only knows it with the whole of her body, the way a deer knows to stand frozen in the grass.

The silence is enormous.

It is not a lack of sound. She has known quiet before, in the Hall, in the Roll Room, in a sickroom at four in the morning. This is different. This is a silence with weight and edges, a silence that presses against the eardrums like water at the bottom of a lake. It has a texture. It has an appetite. Somewhere in it a lamp should hum and a boat should creak and four living people should be breathing, and none of those sounds comes to her at all.

Jian lowers the staff, very slowly, to the stone. He turns his head. He lifts his right hand, flat, and then touches two fingers to his lips and shakes his head.

No speech.

She nods.

* * *

Somewhere on the boat, she thinks, she has begun to remember him.

It comes in pieces, like the others: a hand rubbing tired eyes, a stooped back, a smell of ink and warm paper. In the Year 3, in the raw cavern where they raised the ring, there had been a heavy man with a stoop who sat on an upturned crate in the rain and drew. He drew on everything. Paper, slate, the backs of other people's plans. He drew the cavern's walls and the Gate's fire and the long thin line of the Seam. He had called it a habit. He had said a man who has nothing to fix should at least see what is broken.

The Cartographer, she had thought, and had been fond of him.

Now, standing on a plain of silent stone with the dead Ferryman's cloak behind her, she wonders what he would have drawn of the last six hundred years.

The Fourth Terrace is a field of statues, and the statues are watching.

That is her first impression, and it does not leave her. They stand in rows across a plain of pale gray dust, as far as the lantern's reach and farther, hundreds upon hundreds of them, carved in a stone the color of old bone. Men and women, old and young, in the plain gowns of the Hall's early days. Some stand with their hands at their sides. Some lean on staves. Some are caught mid-stride with one foot lifted, or kneeling, or bent over a tool. There is a woman with a basket on her hip. There is a boy with a kite. There is a bearded man frozen in the act of calling to someone, his mouth open, his head thrown back.

They are not weathered. They are not cracked. Every fold of cloth, every eyelash, every wrinkle at the corner of a smiling mouth has been preserved with a terrible fidelity, as though the people had been caught in the instant before a breath and turned to stone from the inside out.

Hua walks among them, slowly, with Mo Yan's hand in hers. She does not look at the faces. She knows what she would see.

Keepers, she thinks. Every one.

The Book of the Garden had said it: no one has come down from it in two hundred years. It had not said why. It had said only that the Fourth Terrace was a thing the Keepers of the lower rings did not discuss. Now she understands why. It is not that the Fourth is cruel or strange. It is that it is full of people who are still here.

She feels a small cold hand tug hers.

Mo Yan has stopped beside a statue. It is a girl, perhaps nine, in a plain gray gown, with a broken doll in her arms. Her face is turned up. Her mouth is a little open, as if she were about to say something. There are tears on her cheeks, carved with such care that Hua half expects them to roll.

Mo Yan lifts her free hand, shaking, and signs. She is warm.

Hua stares at her.

She is warm, signs the girl again. Her fingers tremble. Feel.

Hua reaches out, hesitates, and lays two fingers on the stone girl's shoulder.

It is warm.

Not hot. Not feverish. Warm as the shoulder of a child who has been asleep in the sun. Beneath the pale surface there is a faint slow pulse, so slow it is almost not there, a single beat that comes and goes like the tide.

She snatches her hand back. Her heart is hammering. She looks at Jian across the field of statues and sees that he has done the same. He is standing beside the bearded man with his mouth open, and his palm is flat on the man's chest, and his face has gone the color of the stone.

They are alive, he signs. The Lin sign for life is two fingers over the heart. His hand is trembling so badly the gesture is hard to read. All of them. Asleep.

* * *

It takes Hua an hour to understand the rule, and Mo Yan understands it first.

The girl has been standing at the edge of the field, near the quay, with her head cocked and her eyes shut. She does it often now: the stillness that means she is listening to something the rest of them cannot hear. When she opens her eyes she crosses the dust to Hua's side and tugs her sleeve, and when Hua bends, Mo Yan takes her wrist in one small hand and places it, with great care, against her own throat.

Hua feels the pulse there. Fast, thin, frightened. And under it, very faint, a hum.

The sound, signs Mo Yan. She pauses. She searches for the words, her hands moving in short stuttering arcs. Words go into the ground. The ground keeps them. If you speak, it takes the voice. Then it takes the one who spoke.

Takes? signs Hua.

Makes stone. The girl's fingers shake. It is not cruel. It is hungry. The Terrace was made to eat sound. To keep it from going up.

Hua looks at the rows of silent figures. At the bearded man with his open mouth. At the stone girl with her doll.

They spoke, she signs. They called out.

They screamed. Mo Yan's eyes are enormous. When it started. When the Bloom came. They screamed, and the ground took the scream, and it took them.

The Bloom came here?

Not the Bloom. The sound of it. Mo Yan's hands are moving faster now, in jerks. It was loud. It was the loudest thing in the world. It shook the whole road. And the Keepers of the Fourth knew that if it climbed, it would wake everything above. So they...

She stops. Her hands fall to her sides.

Hua finishes it, slowly, with the cold creeping up her spine. They let the ground take them. On purpose. To be a wall.

Mo Yan nods.

A wall of living stone, four hundred Keepers deep, each holding the scream of a world in their throat so that it could not go up the stair. Two hundred years of silence. No one had come down because no one could. They were not dead. They were busy.

Hua puts her hand over her mouth and finds that her eyes are streaming.

* * *

Jian signs the plan in the dust.

He kneels at the edge of the quay with the staff laid across his knees and draws with his finger in the gray powder, a crooked map: the quay, the field, the far edge of the Terrace where a pale arch glimmers against the dark. A line of lamps leads from the quay to the arch, he draws, a winding path between the rows of statues, and along the path, at intervals, he scratches small crosses.

Ward points, he signs. The Interface sees them. If we keep to the path and make no sound, we cross. Four hundred paces.

And the sound? signs Hua.

The ground takes what falls on it. He makes a swift, flat gesture. Footsteps are small. They are forgiven. Voices are not. Even a whisper.

Mo Yan's bell.

He looks down. The girl has the little black glass bell in her fist, the Ferryman's gift. Her knuckles are white. Jian shakes his head, once, slowly.

Do not ring it, he signs. Not here.

She nods. She tucks it into the bosom of her gown and presses her hand over it, as one might over a bird.

Mo Yan stays beside the stone girl with the broken doll longer than she should.

Hua sees her from the path. The child is kneeling in the dust with both hands pressed against the cold hem of the gray gown, her head bowed. Her lips are moving, silently, shaping the Ferryman's old tune with no breath behind it. A single tear falls from her chin and does not make a sound as it strikes the stone.

For a long time nothing happens. Then, very faintly, the carved tears on the statue's cheek seem to shine, the way wet glass shines when a candle passes behind it. A flicker of warmth runs through the pale surface. The stone fingers on the doll's arm, for an instant, curl.

Mo Yan jerks back. Her hands fly to her mouth.

She heard, the girl signs, trembling, as Hua reaches her. She heard me.

Heard what?

The song. Her eyes are huge. It does not need a voice. It is a thing in the chest.

Hua folds her into her arms and holds her hard. She says nothing. She cannot. Over the small braided head she sees Jian watching, with the staff lowered and the Interface's pale unfocused look in his eyes, and sees him slowly, deliberately nod.

Later, he signs. We will come back with the song.

They go in single file, as quietly as breath. Jian leads, with his staff held carefully an inch above the dust so that it will not tap. Mo Yan follows, small and silent, one hand trailing along the cloaks of the statues as if to reassure them. Hua comes last. Her mark is dark and cold on her palm. She does not look at it.

Pebble rides on Jian's shoulder with her scales pressed flat. I do not like this, she says. Hua cannot hear her. She sees the little beast's black bead eyes dart over the rows of stone faces and knows, as clearly as if the creature had spoken, that she is saying it.

* * *

They are halfway across when they find the first of the Sect's party.

He stands in the middle of the path, a young man in gray silk, caught in the act of drawing a sword. His left hand holds the scabbard. His right is raised, frozen, with the blade half out. His face is a mask of such astonishment that Hua's stomach turns over.

One of Ming Xue's, signs Jian, his fingers shaking. The tall one.

How long?

Hours. He bends, and presses his palm to the young man's chest, and shuts his eyes. Warm still. The stone is only to the skin. He is... He hesitates, searching. Not yet gone. Not yet fixed. He could be woken.

How?

I do not know.

Hua stares at the drawn sword. At the stone eyes, wide with surprise, fixed on something to the left of the path. She turns her head and looks.

There is a second statue, a few paces off. A woman in gray silk, kneeling, with her hands over her ears. And a third beyond her. And a fourth, a fifth, a sixth.

All six.

They stand scattered across the field in attitudes of horror, each frozen where the ground caught them. The Sect's advance party. Seven in all, with the Elder who led them, and six of them have been turned to stone in the time it took Hua's boat to cross the lake.

They spoke, signs Jian, very small.

Ye Shuhan told them to wait for us. Hua cannot stop shaking. He told them to stay on the quay. They would have... He must have known...

Perhaps not.

He knew. Her hands snap the words. He walked through here in silence. He has a chart. He knew the rule. He left six young people to learn it with their lives.

Jian does not answer. He kneels in the gray dust beside the nearest statue, a girl no older than Cheng Hui, and lays his trembling hand on her stone cheek. His face is bleak.

We will come back for them, he signs.

How?

I do not know yet. He draws a slow breath. But I will not leave them.

* * *

At the third lamp, she nearly dies.

She does not see it. She is walking with her eyes on the arch, one foot after the other, her mind a long way off, and she steps a hand's breadth to the left of the path to avoid a statue's trailing sleeve. The ground gives a soft sigh. A circle of pale light flares round her boot, hair-fine, humming, and the dust at her feet begins to move.

She cannot cry out. She does not have to. A hand closes on her wrist and hauls.

Jian has come back down the path faster than she thought a man with a staff and two shaking hands could move. He yanks her out of the circle and into his chest, and they both go down in the dust together, rolling, silent. The light flares white behind them. The ground ripples. A slow pale tongue of stone licks up out of the dust where she stood, taller than a man, and curls in the air like a wave about to break.

Then it sinks. It sinks back into the dust without a sound, as if nothing had happened, and the circle goes dark.

They lie there. Jian's chest is going like a bellows against her shoulder. His hands are clenched in her gown and shaking so hard she can feel them through the wool. His face, an inch from hers, is white and slick with sweat, and his eyes are fixed on the third lamp.

Sorry, he signs, with his chin pressed to her collarbone. I should have said.

You said. She is trembling too. I did not look.

Lin tremor. A ghost of a grin. It runs in the family.

She does not laugh. She presses her face into his shoulder, for one moment, as one would with a brother. Then she gets up, and brushes the dust from her knees, and they go on.

The Interface speaks to Jian, she learns later, as they pass the stone girl with the doll.

He tells her in signs, in the cold gray quiet of the arch, with the dust still caked on his sleeve. It had said: Terrace Four is a quarantine. The sleepers are not statues. They are suspended patterns, held in place by the sound they swallowed. To wake one, the sound must be given back. It had said: Return requires a voice that is not afraid. And then, in the small flat letters it uses for things it does not yet understand: This unit has never recorded a quarantine that was also a cradle.

Cradle, Hua signs, frowning.

It means they are safe. His hands move slowly. Not dead. Not harmed. Kept, like the Seven, until someone can ask.

And if no one asks?

Then they wait. His mouth twists. We are very good at waiting, in this family.

The arch is a hundred paces away when Hua hears the voice.

It does not come from a statue. It does not come from the ground. It comes from inside her skull, clear and soft and entirely unmistakable, and it speaks her name.

Warden.

She freezes. Her heart stops.

Do not be afraid, says the voice. It is a man's, mild, dry, a little hoarse. It has the faintly apologetic cadence of a man who has spent too long alone and is not sure he remembers how to be heard. I have been waiting for you. I could not speak aloud. The ground would take it. But the mark in your hand can carry a thought, if you let it.

Who are you? Hua thinks. She is shaking so hard she can barely stand.

You know me.

I do not.

You do. A pause. I was always rubbing my eyes. You said I would wear a hole in my face. I said a man who draws maps for a living is entitled to a little eyestrain.

Hua's knees give way.

She sits down in the dust. She does not decide to. She is aware of Jian turning, and Mo Yan, white-faced, reaching for her. She is aware of her own hand, the one with the mark, burning like a coal on her knee. And she is aware of a figure at the far edge of the Terrace, a hundred paces away, standing in the open arch with a bandaged hand lifted in greeting.

It is a heavy man, bent at the shoulders, in a long gray cloak. His face is broad and kind and deeply lined, and he is rubbing his eyes.

The Cartographer, she thinks.

Yes, says the voice. I am sorry about the dust. I did not mean to frighten you. Come across. Slowly. Mind the third lamp; it is a trap.

Hua staggers to her feet.

You are alive.

In a manner of speaking. A soft, rueful chuckle, inside her head. I am the last Keeper of the Fourth Terrace. The rest are asleep. I have been keeping them for two hundred years, and I am more tired than I can say.

You drew the map, she thinks. The one the Sect used.

I drew all the maps. The voice is gentle. That is what I was for. I drew the road, and the Terraces, and the doors. And when the Tenth went up, he asked me for a copy, and I gave it to him, because I did not know what he wanted it for. A pause. I know now.

What does he want?

To be relieved. The Cartographer's voice thins. That is what the shadow told you, is it not? The Stair-Father is tired. He has held the top of the Seam for six hundred years, alone, and he can hold it no longer. He wants someone to come up the road and take his place. A silence like a held breath. He did not think it through. A man who has been alone that long cannot think. He sent the key down, and the map, and the shadow, and he waited. And the one who came was not the one he wanted.

Ye Shuhan.

A good man in a bad robe. The chuckle again, sad now. He thinks the Stair-Father is a god. He thinks the road ends in ascension. He is going to the top to be told he has done well.

And he will find?

A tired old man with a broken heart. The black eyes across the dust are very kind. And a Seam that is not holding. A pause. But he is not what I wished to warn you of. I have very bad news, I am afraid. It concerns the one who is coming down the stair.

Not Ye Shuhan?

No.

The gray figure in the arch drops its hand.

Someone worse, says the Cartographer. Someone who has not been awake in six hundred years.

And behind him, in the shadow of the arch, a second shape unfolds from the dark: tall, slender, hooded, with a bandaged hand held against its chest. It lifts its head. It looks across the hundred paces of gray dust, straight into Hua's eyes, and she sees, even at that distance, the faint ember glow of a ring with a gap and nine spokes.

Oh, thinks Hua, with a calm that frightens her. It is the other key.

She does not look away. Beside her Jian's hand finds her sleeve, and Mo Yan's finds the other, and the three of them stand in the silent dust among the sleeping stone, waiting for whatever the second key has come down the stair to say.
